x.A: A private endpoint is reachable only from within a VPC through interface endpoints, so geographically distributed internet users can't use it.
x.B: A Regional endpoint serves clients in a single Region and doesn't route users through edge locations, so users far from the Region see higher latency.
x.C: An interface VPC endpoint is a way to reach AWS services privately from a VPC and isn't an API Gateway endpoint type for public users.
x.D: An edge-optimized endpoint routes requests through CloudFront edge locations, which reduces latency for geographically distributed clients.

x.A: A CloudFront security policy sets the minimum TLS protocol version and ciphers. It doesn't create certificates.
x.B: Origin access control restricts access to an S3 origin. It doesn't create certificates.
x.C: ACM issues public certificates and renews them automatically when DNS validation is used, because the validation record stays in place. It integrates with CloudFront with no manual work.
x.D: Email validation requires someone to respond to an email, which can break automatic renewal and adds manual work.

x.A: DAX is a fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that takes read latency from milliseconds to microseconds. It's API compatible, so it needs very little change and effort.
x.B: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics and doesn't give microsecond reads.
x.C: RDS isn't faster than DynamoDB for this and would require a full migration.
x.D: ElastiCache for Redis would need application code to manage caching, which is more overhead than DAX.

x.A: Instance Scheduler on AWS starts and stops RDS instances on a schedule, so the database doesn't run nights and weekends, which saves cost with little operational work.
x.B: Turning off automated backups and taking weekly snapshots doesn't reduce the instance cost and puts data at risk.
x.C: A custom Lambda function based on CPU utilization is more code to maintain than the Instance Scheduler.
x.D: All Upfront reserved DB instances give a discount for 24/7 use, but the application is idle most of the week, so you'd pay for unused time.

x.A: FSx for Lustre is for high-performance computing and would change the storage architecture, and an Auto Scaling group adds changes.
x.B: A gp2 volume works as block storage, but gp3 has lower cost per GB and better baseline performance.
x.C: FSx for OpenZFS is a file system, which changes the architecture and costs more than an EBS volume.
x.D: A gp3 EBS volume is the closest replacement for locally attached block storage, with low latency, and it's the lower-cost, higher-baseline option compared with gp2. It needs no architecture change.

x.A: Two instances in two AZs meet the minimum, but if one AZ fails, only one instance would run until a replacement launches, so at least two instances aren't always running.
x.B: A minimum of four with two instances in each of two AZs means two instances are still running if an AZ fails, so the requirement holds. On-Demand Instances avoid interruptions for a stateful application.
x.C: Spot Instances in a single AZ can be reclaimed and an AZ failure would take everything down.
x.D: Spot Instances can be interrupted, so two instances aren't guaranteed at all times.

x.A: Geolocation routing directs by the user's location rather than by lowest latency, and users near neither location may not match a rule. It doesn't minimize load time as well.
x.B: Simple routing has no location logic and can't route traffic based on proximity.
x.C: A latency routing policy sends each user to the endpoint with the lowest latency. Associating the records with us-west-1 for the on-premises data center and eu-central-1 minimizes load time.
x.D: Weighted routing splits traffic by weight without regard for user location, so many users reach the farther site.

x.A: Reading 5 PB from tapes, staging in NFS, and sending with DataSync over a 1 Gbps link would take years, since 5 PB would take over a year at full speed.
x.B: Writing 5 PB directly to Glacier Deep Archive over 1 Gbps would also take far too long.
x.C: Snowball devices with Tape Gateway let you copy tapes to virtual tapes offline and ship them to AWS, which meets the 6 month deadline. Then a lifecycle policy moves them to Deep Archive, the cheapest class for 10 year retention.
x.D: A Tape Gateway over the 1 Gbps internet connection is too slow for 5 PB in 6 months.

x.A: A spread placement group puts each instance on distinct underlying hardware, so nodes don't share the same hardware.
x.B: Separate accounts don't control whether instances share underlying hardware.
x.C: Dedicated tenancy keeps your instances on hardware dedicated to your account, but your own instances can still share the same hardware among themselves.
x.D: Shared tenancy places instances on shared hardware and doesn't separate groups of nodes.

x.A: On-Demand Instances don't guarantee capacity, because capacity can be unavailable when you need it.
x.B: A Savings Plan is a billing discount and doesn't reserve capacity.
x.C: Regional Reserved Instances give a billing discount but don't reserve capacity in a specific AZ.
x.D: A Capacity Reservation reserves EC2 capacity in the failover Region, so the DR strategy is guaranteed capacity when needed.

x.A: An account can't belong to two organizations at the same time.
x.B: The R&D account first has to leave the prior organization. Then the new management account can invite it to join the new organization.
x.C: Creating a new account and migrating resources takes a lot of work, and isn't needed because accounts can be moved between organizations.
x.D: A management account can't be a member of another organization, and it doesn't make sense to join both.

x.A: A Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting virtual appliances into traffic and doesn't handle authorization, and EFS isn't suited for analytics ingestion.
x.B: A Lambda function for authorization is possible, but the proper integrated feature is an API Gateway Lambda authorizer, and the ingestion into S3 would be done through Firehose.
x.C: API Gateway scales for sudden bursts, a Lambda authorizer handles authorization, and Firehose delivers the data to S3 for analytics. All are managed.
x.D: A GWLB doesn't terminate or authorize API requests, and this design is over-engineered.

x.A: A cross-Region read replica runs a second instance all the time, which costs more than needed for a 24 hour RPO and RTO.
x.B: DMS replication needs a replication instance running continuously and more setup.
x.C: RDS native backups to S3 need manual handling, and copying them is more work than copying snapshots.
x.D: Copying automated snapshots to another Region once a day meets a 24 hour RPO, and restoring takes within the 24 hour RTO. It has no running secondary instance, so it's the cheapest.

x.A: Memcached has no replication or persistence, so session data is lost if a node fails.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis stores session data outside the web servers, and with replication and Multi-AZ failover the data survives a node failure, so sessions aren't lost when a web server goes down.
x.C: A Storage Gateway cached volume isn't a session store for web servers and wouldn't work for sharing session state.
x.D: RDS can store session state, but it's slower and costlier for frequent small reads and writes than Redis.

x.A: A read replica handles the monthly report queries so the primary keeps its performance for the daily workload.
x.B: Restoring a backup to another instance gives only a point-in-time copy and is a manual process each month.
x.C: Exporting data to S3 and querying with Athena takes more work and the data isn't current.
x.D: Resizing the instance to cover a monthly peak means paying for extra capacity all the time.

x.A: An NLB works at layer 4, so it can't route requests to different microservices based on URL paths.
x.B: The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an ALB from Kubernetes Ingress resources, and an ALB routes requests by path or host to the right microservice. It's cost-effective.
x.C: A Lambda function to route requests means custom code and extra cost.
x.D: API Gateway can route requests but costs more per request and adds another service.

x.A: A public bucket link exposes the images to anyone, which doesn't protect copyrighted images or deny countries, and MFA doesn't apply to links.
x.B: Creating an IAM user for each customer doesn't scale and doesn't give fast global access or country restrictions.
x.C: EC2 instances storing images in each country costs far more and has a lot of management.
x.D: S3 stores the images cheaply, CloudFront delivers them quickly worldwide, geographic restrictions deny users from specific countries, and signed URLs limit access to paying customers.

x.A: Multi-AZ replication groups with multiple nodes per shard give node-level and AZ-level failover, and data is replicated so failures don't lose data or degrade performance.
x.B: AOF turns on persistence on a node but doesn't provide failover across AZs, and AOF isn't supported with Multi-AZ replication groups on newer versions.
x.C: A Multi-AZ replication group with more than one replica is similar, but the question expects shards that contain multiple nodes for the complete design.
x.D: Auto Scaling changes capacity and doesn't provide failover at the node or Region level.

x.A: Starting more instances doesn't reduce the time each instance takes to load memory and become productive.
x.B: Spot Instances don't reduce launch time and can be interrupted.
x.C: Hibernation saves the instance's memory state to the root volume, so a resumed instance returns to its loaded state quickly. Auto Scaling warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready, which cuts launch time.
x.D: Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity but don't shorten the time to load the application.

x.A: Manual scaling requires someone to react, so it wouldn't keep up with sudden traffic increases on random days.
x.B: Predictive scaling forecasts regular patterns from history, so it doesn't help with random, unpredictable spikes.
x.C: Dynamic scaling reacts to metrics like CPU or request count and adds capacity when traffic rises, which handles random spikes and avoids paying for idle capacity.
x.D: Scheduled scaling works for known times, but the spikes happen on random days.

x.A: Aurora Serverless v2 is PostgreSQL compatible and scales capacity automatically with demand, so it handles unpredictable spikes and you pay only for what you use.
x.B: EC2 doesn't offer auto scaling for a single database instance, because scaling a database that way isn't simple.
x.C: A larger RDS instance type costs more all the time to cover a monthly peak.
x.D: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics, and wouldn't suit a transactional ecommerce database.

x.A: API Gateway throttling limits control request rates and don't reduce cold start latency.
x.B: Scheduled scaling for provisioned concurrency has Lambda environments initialized before employees start work, so the first requests of the day don't face cold starts.
x.C: A CloudWatch alarm doesn't have a time schedule and would invoke after the fact.
x.D: More memory can speed up execution, but it doesn't remove cold starts at the start of the day.

x.A: An S3 File Gateway on premises presents an SMB file share that the devices write to, and the files are stored in S3, so the data lands in the cloud with no changes to the devices.
x.B: FSx File Gateway connects to FSx for Windows File Server, which costs more, and isn't needed to query .csv files with SQL.
x.C: A Glue crawler infers the schema of the .csv files in S3 and creates a table in the Data Catalog, which lets Athena query them.
x.D: An EMR cluster for periodic queries costs more and needs more management than Athena.
x.E: Redshift is more costly to run for periodic queries, and it needs a cluster.
x.F: Athena queries data in S3 with SQL, serverless and pay-per-query, so it's cost-effective for periodic queries.

x.A: The customer provides resilient power and network connectivity to the Outposts racks at their site.
x.B: AWS manages the virtualization hypervisor, storage systems, and the AWS services that run on Outposts.
x.C: The customer is responsible for physical security and access controls of the data center where Outposts are installed.
x.D: AWS is responsible for the availability of the Outposts infrastructure, including power supplies, servers, and networking equipment inside the racks.
x.E: AWS handles physical maintenance of Outposts components.
x.F: The customer provides extra capacity for ECS clusters, so they can handle server failures and maintenance events.

x.A: An NLB handles TCP on any port at millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, so it matches the hardware appliance's performance.
x.B: An ALB is for HTTP and HTTPS at layer 7 and has higher latency, and it doesn't support arbitrary TCP applications.
x.C: CloudFront only listens on HTTP and HTTPS ports, and not on nonstandard TCP ports.
x.D: API Gateway handles HTTP and WebSocket APIs, not raw TCP on a nonstandard port, and wouldn't give the same performance.
